case_info.scenario: An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

dialogue_history.text: While combination therapy is indeed a standard approach for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), this patient's specific history raises critical safety concerns. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is associated with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs), and initiating endothelin receptor antagonists like ambrisentan can increase the risk of serious hemorrhage. The next essential step before starting any PAH-specific therapy is to perform a contrast echocardiogram (bubble study) or CT angiography to rule out PAVMs, as their presence would drastically alter management.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

  }
}

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

[Role]

next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.

- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

[Case]
An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. After PTE, more than 95% of patients have substantial improvements in functional status and cardiac index and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure; 1-year survival is up to 95%.8However, up to one-third of patients with CTEPH are not candidates for PTE due to surgically inaccessible thrombi or comorbidities.8Balloon pulmonary angioplasty, a percutaneous vascular procedure that involves balloon inflation of narrowed pulmonary arteries, may be considered for patients with inoperable CTEPH.7,9Riociguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, is the only medication approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for CTEPH. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). RHC revealed a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 48 mm Hg (reference, ≤20 mm Hg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 8 mm Hg (reference, ≤15 mm Hg), and cardiac index 2.0 L/min/m2(reference, 2.2-4.0 L/min/m2). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. At a clinic visit 6 months after presentation, the patient reported decreased dyspnea, and his lower extremity edema had diminished to the ankles bilaterally. Brain-type natriuretic peptide level had decreased to 760 pg/mL, and a repeat echocardiogram revealed a reduction in right ventricular systolic pressure, to 50 to 55 mm Hg.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

case_info.explanation: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) B. Obtain a ventilation/perfusion (V̇/Q̇) lung scan. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that CTEPH is a cause of pulmonary hypertension that should be suspected in a patient with a history of pulmonary embolism. Vasodilator therapy (choice A) is not indicated unless CTEPH has been excluded and pulmonary arterial hypertension is confirmed on right heart catheterization (RHC). Although CT pulmonary angiogram (choice C) is useful to characterize vascular involvement, V̇/Q̇ scan is the preferred initial diagnostic test for CTEPH. Intravenous bevacizumab (choice D) is used to treat epistaxis and high-output heart failure in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and would not be appropriate for this patient. Pulmonary hypertension is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg at rest and is classified into 5 groups.1CTEPH is categorized as pulmonary hypertension group 4 and is caused by organized thromboemboli that obstruct pulmonary blood flow and cause pericapillary microvasculopathy.2,3The worldwide annual incidence of CTEPH is estimated at 5 per million individuals and prevalence is approximately 38 per million, although CTEPH is likely underdiagnosed.3CTEPH develops in less than 4% of patients diagnosed with an acute pulmonary embolism.4However, at least 25% of patients with CTEPH have no known history of pulmonary embolism.3Risk factors for CTEPH include malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, elevated factor VIII levels, chronic inflammatory diseases (eg, inflammatory bowel disease), hypothyroidism, and splenectomy.5In a study of 679 consecutive patients with CTEPH, common presenting symptoms were dyspnea (99%), peripheral edema (40.5%), fatigue (31.5%), chest pain (15.3%), and syncope (13.7%).6 All patients with pulmonary hypertension should be evaluated with a V̇/Q̇ scan, which has a sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 91%, and negative predictive value of 98% for pulmonary embolism.2,5If mismatched perfusion defects are identified on V̇/Q̇ scan, a CT pulmonary angiogram should be performed to further visualize the pulmonary vasculature. All patients with pulmonary hypertension should undergo RHC to evaluate mean pulmonary artery pressure before initiating therapy.7 The treatment of choice for CTEPH is pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE), a surgical procedure that involves median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass to remove organized thrombi from the pulmonary arteries. Patients with inoperable CTEPH or recurrent pulmonary hypertension after PTE had significantly improved functional capacity and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance after riociguat treatment.2,10All patients with CTEPH should receive lifelong anticoagulation, if not contraindicated. A V̇/Q̇ scan showed bilateral mismatched perfusion defects (Figure, panel A). A CT pulmonary angiogram showed eccentric filling defects in the lobar and segmental pulmonary arterial branches of the lower lobes bilaterally (Figure, panel B). After discussion with the surgical team, a decision was made not to pursue PTE due to the patient’s comorbidities and deconditioned status. He was treated with riociguat (2.5 mg 3 times daily) and declined anticoagulation due to prior epistaxis while taking warfarin. You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 82-year-old with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and history of past cigarette smoking presented to pulmonary clinic for evaluation of dyspnea that had worsened over the previous 5 years. Two years prior, he was diagnosed with a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism on a computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram after evaluation of shortness of breath. Warfarin was initiated but discontinued after 2 months due to recurrent epistaxis. On presentation to the pulmonary clinic, the patient reported dyspnea with minimal activity, fatigue, lightheadedness, and leg swelling. His temperature was 96.8 °F (36 °C); blood pressure, 120/71 mm Hg; heart rate, 73/min; and oxygen saturation, 98% on room air. He appeared frail and had multiple telangiectasias on his lips, tongue, and hands. He had jugular venous distension, a cardiac systolic murmur, right ventricular heave, and bilateral lower extremity edema to the knees. Laboratory testing revealed brain-type natriuretic peptide level of 1333 pg/mL (reference, <100 pg/mL) and hemoglobin level of 12.9 g/dL (reference, 13.9-16.3 g/dL). During a 6-minute walk test on room air, his oxygen saturation decreased to 87%. With oxygen delivered by nasal cannula at 4 L/min, his oxygen saturation was 98%, and he walked 90 m (15% of predicted). An echocardiogram showed a normal left ventricular ejection fraction, moderate-severe right ventricular dilatation, and right ventricular systolic pressure of 60 to 70 mm Hg (reference, 35-40 mm Hg). Findings on an echocardiogram performed 10 years prior were normal.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 8.4. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
